Scott Bessent is running Washington’s other war department
item.description:
Marco Rubio may be Secretary of State, but the role of top diplomat for Ukraine, Iran and even Gaza was bestowed on two real estate investors, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. And while they manage the diplomacy portfolio, the Treasury Department is waging war.

At Treasury’s helm is former Wall Street investor and hedge fund manager Scott Bessent. Now the warrior banker, he uses tariffs as threats and sanctions as bombs.

The Trump administration has repeatedly threatened Canada with talk of becoming the 51st state. Handing the file to Bessent, Trump announced that the U.S. would use “economic force” to “get rid of that artificially drawn line” between Canada and the United States.

When the Canadian province of Alberta held a referendum on whether they wanted a future referendum on independence, Bessent intervened, saying Alberta would make a perfect partner for the United States. He said Ottawa is frustrating Alberta and its “wealth of natural resources” by not letting it “build a pipeline to the Pacific.” As a solution, he suggested that “we should let them come down into the U.S…. Alberta is a natural partner for the U.S. They have great resources. The Albertans are very independent people." The preliminary referendum was overwhelmingly defeated.

Not wanting boots on the ground in Cuba, Trump turned the Cuba file over to Treasury before the Pentagon. The economic strangulation of Cuba has not toppled the Cuban government, but it has devastated its people. The island is in darkness, and water, food, and medicine are scarce. Tens of thousands of surgeries have been canceled. According to U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk, “children are dying because doctors lack access to essential medical supplies and medicines.”

Employing a strategy of “carrot and stick,” Bessent said sanctions can go up or down depending on the behavior of the Cuban government. The U.N. says Washington’s sanctions are “incompatible with basic principles of international human rights law.” Bessent’s evaluation is that they are working: “It is working in Cuba right now… we are going to bring this regime down.”

Bessent says that, as the strategy is working in Cuba, so it will work in Iran. "Operation Economic Outcast" was supposed to land the killer blow on Iran (and anyone doing business with Iran). And, according to Bessent’s metrics, it did. Even before the war Bessent said, “President Trump ordered… maximum pressure on Iran. And it worked, because in December, their economy collapsed... and this is why the people took to the street.” Bessent told the Senate Banking Committee that “what we have done is created a dollar shortage in the country… The Iranian currency went into free fall, inflation exploded, and hence we have seen the Iranian people out on the street.”

Fast forward to Sunday, Bessant said that the projected 25% contraction of the Iranian economy is “one of the fastest collapses in history” and boasted that “everything I’m doing is working.”

The force of Bessent’s economic war machine received validation from the State Department on November 10, when Rubio assessed that the military war on Iran was no longer necessary because economic war was working better. "The economic pain that is being inflicted on Iran right now is extraordinary,” Rubio told G7 leaders. "We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure.” Bessent had been lobbying Trump to take that route.

Of course the Iranians, who after eight months of are still hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and attacking neighbors in the Gulf, like Bahrain, in retaliation for U.S. strikes, might have a word or two to say about that. "Despite all these pressures, the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion,” Central Bank chief Abdolnaser Hemmati said in October.

The leader of the campaign to negotiate with Iran, meanwhile, has been Vice President JD Vance, who was recently speaking almost every day to Qatari and Pakistani mediators. At the end of October, Vance sent a letter to the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, exploring the possibility of direct talks to stave off the resumption of intense attacks by the U.S.

But two days after Rubio’s endorsement of economic warfare, Trump signed off on it, pulling Vance off the file. Relying on Bessent’s economic approach, Trump said, “we don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

American foreign policy evolution has in the last 25 years favored the Pentagon and the CIA over the State Department. During the two Trump administrations, as Washington has fully appreciated the power of its dollar dominance and control of trade networks and payment systems, the Treasury has risen to join the two predominant agencies, with Bessent at its helm.

But that doesn’t mean a kinder, gentler form of foreign policy. A landmark study published in The Lancet by Francisco Rodríguez, Silvio Rendón, and Mark Weisbrot found that unilateral U.S. sanctions are associated with death tolls similar to armed conflict. The prevailing weapons may have changed, but the results are all about punishment with very little room for diplomacy or progress toward peace.

item.title: US keeps punishing Iraq to get at Iran
item.description:
Washington’s latest attempt to restrict Iraq’s economic relations with Iran exposes a serious contradiction in the U.S. approach toward Baghdad.

While Washington seeks to establish an expanded bilateral partnership following the withdrawal of its forces from Iraq, it continues to push Baghdad to become part of Washington’s confrontation with Tehran. This policy risks strengthening those political forces in Iraq that Washington seeks to weaken.

On November 8, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein revealed that the U.S. Treasury had demanded the closure of all but two border crossings with Iran. This in turn followed Trump’s alleged threat to strike Iraqi armed factions if they participated in renewed fighting on behalf of Iran.

Earlier in October, the Treasury imposed sanctions on an Iraqi bank accused of facilitating Iranian sanctions evasion and supporting armed organizations. Earlier measures targeted militia commanders and individuals allegedly exploiting Iraq's oil industry.

But Iran retains an enduring influence in Iraq, a result of both geography and close historical and religious ties. More important is the question of security. Iraq neither can nor wants to serve as Washington’s, or indeed anyone’s, military bulwark against Iran. This thinking has further solidified in Baghdad amid the ongoing war in which Iran has effectively weathered U.S. pressure.

The U.S. has tried to pull Iraq away from Iran under previous Iraqi governments without success. But the latest attempt is driven by the understanding that the current Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, is a politician particularly suited for this kind of mission given his experience as a businessman and his highly transactional approach to foreign policy. Washington also believes that al-Zaidi, as a man hailing from outside the Iraqi political system, would be better able to integrate the Iran-leaning militias into the state.

Yet the problem is that al-Zaidi — having emerged from the Shia Coordination Framework, which includes factions maintaining close relations with Tehran — must balance competing interests while strengthening state institutions. American pressure risks weakening those Iraqi politicians who favor pragmatic cooperation with Washington. Iran-backed factions could portray stringent U.S. demands as evidence that Washington continues to disregard Iraqi sovereignty.

Such arguments may resonate with constituencies that are already critical of decades-long U.S. military operations carried out unilaterally within Iraq’s borders.

Washington appears to believe that disbanding the militias (now postponed by Baghdad to June 2027) would both limit Iran’s influence and benefit Iraq over the longer run. This idea is appealing, but actually carrying it out would not necessarily result in diminishing Tehran’s influence.

Iranian penetration of Iraqi government and society is much greater than just its influence with militias, however powerful they may be. The country’s ministries and other state institutions are packed with bureaucrats and politicians imbued with strong pro-Iranian sentiment. The web of financial and political links between the two countries is such that the notion of “freeing” Iraq from Iran by “disbanding the militias” reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of their relationship.

Limiting Iran’s influence will take a significant amount of time and should ideally go hand in hand with helping create a better investment climate for American and other Western companies. Some moves in this direction have been made. On November 8, Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister for Energy Affairs Mohsen al-Mandalawi met U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Stephen Fagin to discuss implementation of economic agreements worth some $60 billion announced during al-Zaidi's visit to Washington in July.

Promoting closer ties between Iraq on the one hand and Turkey and the Gulf states on the other would also constitute an important step. Syria might not be Iraq’s perfect analogy, but Damascus’ pivot to Turkey and the Gulf states after the fall of the Assad dynasty clearly reduced Iran’s influence there.

Increasing pressure on Iraq over its close ties with Iran at this moment, when U.S. efforts to defeat Iran militarily have clearly fallen short, appears especially ill-timed. The Islamic Republic might be economically highly vulnerable because of Washington’s blockade and tightening sanctions regime, but the country appears to have weathered the external threat. Iran’s neighbors are now more hesitant to pressure the Islamic Republic, which has also managed to reconstitute its military capabilities.

Moreover, Iraq has already suffered substantial economic damage due to disruptions to oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the war. On November 8, Hussein estimated Iraq’s losses from the conflict at approximately $60 billion. Although Iraqi oil exports, which account for approximately 90% of government revenue, recovered to around 3.5 million barrels per day in October, compared with 2.65 million in September, the deterioration in government revenues has exposed the country's structural vulnerabilities. Further restrictions on cross-border commerce would impose additional costs on an economy with limited capacity to absorb them.

Economic relations with Iran are also far more extensive than Washington’s demands appear to acknowledge. Bilateral trade reached approximately $12 billion in Iran’s fiscal year ending in March 2025. The Kurdistan region alone reportedly conducts approximately $5 billion in annual trade with Iran. These commercial connections sustain transportation companies, wholesalers, agricultural producers, merchants, and border communities. Their disruption would affect Iraqi businesses whose operations depend on regular cross-border movement.

Moreover, the consequences could extend beyond conventional trade. Iraq has long relied on Iranian natural gas to fuel electricity generation, even as Baghdad has pursued alternative energy supplies. Economic disengagement from Iran is therefore not simply a matter of political willingness. It requires alternative infrastructure, financing, and supply chains that cannot be established overnight.

The Development Road initiative running from Turkey to the Gulf region via Iraqi territory might also serve as an option that would allow Baghdad to lessen dependence on Iran. But the project’s implementation is still in its early stages, and some accommodation with the Iran-aligned militias over ensuring security along the route will be of critical importance to advance the project.

Thus, continued American efforts to constrain Iraq’s regional engagement risk strengthening precisely those political forces that Washington seeks to weaken. Rather than reducing Iranian influence, political pressure could undermine Iraq’s institutions, encourage anti-American mobilization, and diminish Baghdad's willingness to cooperate with Washington on security and economic issues.

item.title: Will Syria entry into Mecca pact mean clash with the Houthis?
item.description:
Syria appears likely to soon join the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a collective defense agreement established several months ago by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. This development would constitute a milestone in Damascus’ efforts to reassert itself within the region’s security architecture following Syria’s gruesome civil war.

Membership in the pact could enhance the legitimacy and prestige of post-Assad Syria while bolstering its military capabilities and deepening partnerships with influential regional states. Syria could benefit from more intelligence cooperation, military training, and Saudi financial support. All this could complement Damascus’ existing security partnership with Ankara.

But it’s not all milk and honey. Joining the security configuration could expose Syria to foreign conflicts and geopolitical rivalries while undermining Damascus’ ability to prioritize redevelopment at home.

There could also be implications for unresolved problems between Syria’s central government and certain minorities. Such frictions stand to exacerbate if Damascus’ entry into the pact leads to rising sectarian temperatures at home and across the region, particularly within the context of Syrian forces being brought into Saudi Arabia’s conflict with Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa will have to weigh these risks carefully as he decides whether to join the bloc.

Security benefits and military implications for Damascus


Syria faces two main threats today. The most immediate one is Israel, which has expanded its illegal occupation of Syrian territory since the former regime’s fall nearly two years ago. Israeli forces have come within 15 miles of Damascus. Since December 2024, Israel has continued launching strikes on Syrian military infrastructure and seeking to empower separatists in the country despite Sharaa offering the Israelis non-aggression and security agreements.

Iran and its “Axis of Resistance” pose the second threat. From Damascus’ perspective, the risk is that Tehran will intensify pressure on Syria to ensure that the Islamic Republic can continue accessing Lebanon for the purpose of arming Hezbollah within the context of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

At least on paper, accession to the pact could provide Damascus with another layer of deterrence by increasing potential costs for Tel Aviv and Tehran that would come with future acts of aggression against Syria. But the likelihood that the pact’s signatories would actually intervene militarily on behalf of Damascus is anything but guaranteed.

“Membership of the Mecca Agreement will not immediately allay these pressures in direct security terms,” said James Watt, a former British ambassador who now works for a consultancy called Ambassador Partnership LLP. “But Syria can derive an important degree of confidence from the de facto alliance it has created. In the context of rapid changes in regional security structures, Syria has chosen to join the diplomatic centerpiece of the new regional order. The benefits will amplify over time.”

Syria’s ability to make meaningful contributions to the pact is questionable given the degradation of the country’s armed forces and the immense challenges of rebuilding its military institutions. However, Syria’s combat experiences may prove helpful to Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan.

Indications of a growing Saudi-Syrian security partnership include the reported arrival of Syrian military advisers in Saudi Arabia, Syrian plans to deploy roughly 600 special forces personnel to the kingdom, and the new bilateral defense agreement signed on November 4.

“The only place where [Syria] can contribute to a degree is by providing foot soldiers for the Yemen battle front as it does have battle-hardened, experienced and also ideologically motivated former rebel groups who might be relatively more effective in Yemen as compared to any other external force,” said Umar Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies, in an RS interview.

However, Watt believes that such a contribution would mostly serve as a gesture of Syrian solidarity with Saudi Arabia in the Saudi-Houthi conflict.

Regardless, any Syrian deployment to the Arabian Peninsula will divert resources away from the country’s dire domestic needs.

Saudi Arabia's growing stake in Syria


As post-Assad Syria’s most important Arab partner, Saudi Arabia would see Damascus’ membership as enhancing Riyadh’s clout in the Levant and strengthening the kingdom’s security partnerships. Damascus joining the pact would further institutionalize Saudi-Syrian ties and enhance efforts to undermine Iran’s ability to reassert itself in Syria.

Noting a “wider Saudi effort to counter Iranian influence beyond the Gulf,” Elijah J. Magnier, a veteran war correspondent and adviser to the European Parliament’s rapporteur on Iraq and Lebanon, explained that “Assad’s fall weakened Tehran’s position in Syria and gave Riyadh an opening.” Furthermore, by “investing in a long-term relationship with Damascus, Saudi Arabia can help limit Iran’s room to rebuild its influence there while working with Turkey, which already has substantial leverage in Syria.”

Although the Saudi-Syrian defense agreement demonstrates the extent to which Riyadh is committed to its bilateral partnership with Damascus, Magnier stressed that Syrian membership in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement is a separate matter entirely.

“Saudi Arabia would gain a greater stake in the Levant, but it could also face a Syrian request for collective support after Israeli strikes,” he told RS. “Riyadh can advance its strategic interests in Syria through defense cooperation today. Extending a collective guarantee would require it to decide how much risk it is prepared to assume on the Israeli front.”

Where do Turkey and Pakistan stand?


Turkey is Syria’s “natural security partner,” said Watt, who pointed to two countries’ shared historic ties, Sunni identities, and common opposition to Kurdish separatism.

“Within the Agreement, Turkey stands out as having considerable military strength, and through NATO membership an important degree of strategic depth in facing down Israeli threats. In view of all this, the accession of Syria to the agreement seems merely a logical development,” he told RS.

“Israel has chosen to take an aggressive stance towards Turkey, but there is nothing inherent that prevents normal relations were Israel to reverse its expansionist policies in Lebanon, Syria and Palestine,” the former British diplomat added. “Turkey has maintained relations with Tehran in a way that facilitates the diplomatic solution sought by the Mecca Agreement.”

Meanwhile, Islamabad could gain from an enhanced diplomatic and military presence in the Middle East beyond the Gulf. However, Karim argues that “now there does not seem to be much excitement in Pakistan about” Islamabad acquiring “that kind of strategic and diplomatic influence” in Arab states outside the Gulf.

The risk of too many regional entanglements


For all the potential benefits, Syria’s efforts to balance regional relationships could become complicated if Damascus joins the pact. As Watt told RS, Syria’s membership would mark a departure from the neutrality pursued by post-Assad Syria, which could mean less diplomatic flexibility for Sharaa’s government moving forward.

For example, the rivalry between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates raises real concerns about tensions between Damascus and Abu Dhabi resulting from Syrian membership. At the same time, Syria’s relationship with Iran would risk becoming more confrontational should Damascus enter the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.

Ultimately, what remains to be seen is whether the pact’s collective-defense provisions will meaningfully enhance Syria’s security. As Turkey and Pakistan’s responses to Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia since the defense clause’s activation last month underscored, each Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signatory has its own national interests that stand to limit its willingness to become directly involved in conflicts involving its allies. This dynamic should cause officials in Damascus to question what concrete military commitments Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan will make when it comes to defending Syria from Israeli aggression.

America Invented the Drone War, So Why Is It Falling Behind?
item.description:
One mainstream document that called the United States’ sluggish reaction to this Revolution in Military Affairs (RMA) (and did so five years ago) was Christian Brose’s 2019 article in Foreign Affairs, “The New Revolution in Military Affairs: War’s Sci-Fi Future.” Brose’s bottom-line was the following: “Artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, ubiquitous sensors, advanced manufacturing, and quantum science will transform warfare as radically as the technologies that consumed Bloch [a nineteenth-century founder of the concept of RMAs]. And yet the U.S. government’s thinking about how to employ these new technologies is not keeping pace with their development.”

Editorial note: This is the second in a four-part series from former National Geospatial-Intelligence Director VADM Frank Whitworth (Ret.) on the reluctant revolution in military affairs and what it means for future intelligence and defense. This series of perspectives was adapted from a previous white paper written by the author two years ago, while he was on active duty.

Brose correctly identified a history of “change labels” in the last three decades with no resulting or substantial adjustment to core military methods. This trend began with the oncoming “military technical revolution” in 1992, moved to Admiral Arthur Cebrowski’s “Network-Centric Warfare” in the mid-1990s, Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s “transformation” in the 9/11 era, and Deputy Secretary Robert Work’s “third offset strategy” in 2014. Each brought a slight twist on a common theme: “…emerging technologies will enable new battle networks of sensors and shooters to rapidly accelerate the process of detecting, targeting, and striking threats.”

Brose did not stop there. He was critical of American procurement choices over the last three decades as Washington “…poured money into newer versions of old military platforms and prayed for technological miracles to come (which often became acquisition debacles when those miracles did not materialize.” Brose was prescient in identifying how inexpensive uncrewing could be – and how much change it required of the military mindset. Well before Replicator (DOD’s primary development program for autonomous vehicles) became a glimmer in anyone’s eye, Brose identified the need for fleets of drones, with ubiquitous communications and elements of autonomy.

To reiterate, this paper does not intend to prove and explain the United States’ reluctant acceptance of every facet of this “drones, codes, and spacecraft” RMA. In fact, during our application of Marshall’s principles, we cited three major developments that help rule-out our reluctance to accept non-proximate warfare in the space and cyber domains: specifically, the establishment of the United States Space Force, USPACECOM, and USCYBERCOM. Drones are a different matter, though – and to prove our reluctance, we will (a) compare the United States’ rate of “military drone fleet” development to that of Ukraine, and (b) demonstrate the stark difference in DOD’s acquisition budgets between manned and unmanned assets.

Globally, the number of nations with armed drone programs has accelerated. The rapid growth of armed, medium altitude, long endurance (MALE) drones (such as the MQ-9 Reaper) since 2001 is evident in this graphic from Drone Wars UK:

Source: Drone Wars UK

These large, MALE drones are important because they can deliver munitions lengthy distances and damage strategic targets such as infrastructure and headquarters. Since Russia’s invasion in 2022, Ukraine has transformed itself into a world leader of drone technology and employment. In fact, Ukrainian President Zelensky just announced in December 2024 that his country will produce 30,000 MALE drones next year. That nearly triples DOD’s entire drone fleet of 11,000 (a number that even includes smaller, non-MALE assets such as the hand-launched RQ-11B Raven). The United States’ production of military drones has been lapped numerically by Ukraine in only two years—despite America’s 20-year head-start in developing the technology.

The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense Transformation reports seven drone models were produced domestically in 2022, and that number has grown tenfold to 67 in only two years. Similarly, Ukraine now has an astounding 200 domestic drone manufacturers. This stands in stark contrast to America’s drone manufacturing sector, which has declined. With the United States’ withdrawal from Afghanistan and a reduction in military contracts, IBIS World estimates the United States has only 73 businesses in the UAV manufacturing sector. As representationally depicted in Figure 3, the sector is declining at a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 5.8 percent to $4.0 billion through 2024 (dropping 21.4 percent this year alone.)

UAV Manufacturing in the U.S. — Source: IBISWorld

In examining expenditures reported in the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense, Comptroller’s April 4, 2024 report, “Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System, FY2025,” the United States’ reluctance to adopting the “drones” portion of this RMA is demonstrated further. As depicted in Figure 4, unmanned aircraft systems account for less than four percent of DOD’s expenditures dedicated to overall aviation and related systems. Separately, there are no “unmanned” wedges in either the $48 billion of proposed expenditures for shipbuilding and maritime systems or the $13 billion or proposed expenditures for ground systems. To be fair to the Navy, they do lead the other services in Research and Development for unmanned systems – but those investments will require time before they are made manifest in the fleet.

item.title: Where Did the Billions From Venezuela's Oil Go?
item.description:
“We've won Venezuela and [have] taken out billions and billions and billions of dollars already. And we will be taking out many billions of dollars and get along very well. And -- you could call it a territory, you could call it whatever you want. We won that war in less than one hour.”

That was President Trump during his telecast 60 Minutes interview on CBS with Ross Douthat on November 8. However, CBS also has released the transcript of the entire, unedited transcript of the 51-minute interview during which Trump also said, but was not part of the telecast version, “Venezuela, where, by the way, we’ve taken out 50 times what the war has cost already. To the victor belong the spoils.”

I bring up those remarks because last August I wrote a column questioning what had happened to those billions of dollars from Venezuelan oil that Trump referred to many times earlier than the 60 Minutes interview – in fact, Trump began less than a week after the U.S. military seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife on January 3, 2026, and, in effect, took over that country.

Douthat did not ask Trump anything more about the “billions and billions” in the 60 Minutes interview – I wish he had.

Also not discussed was what Trump last August 28 on Truth Social called, “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” where the U.S., through a Pentagon agency, has become the 35 percent owner of what a White House fact sheet called, “the second-largest private oil company by [Venezuelan oil] reserves in the world.”

I will discuss the many still secret parts of that Trump administration deal below.

But the public release last week by the State Department of the American accounting firm KPMG LLP’s 53-page Report on Venezuela Custody Account Operations January - September 2026 October 29, 2026 also failed to answer questions that I and others have raised about what happened to those initial “billions” from Venezuelan oil.

For example, during his January 9, 2026, meeting with oil company leaders at the White House, Trump told the press that was present that Venezuela had already given the U.S. 30 million barrels of what had been previously-sanctioned oil that it had on hand.

“That's about $4 billion worth,” Trump announced back in January, adding, “And it's on our way to the United States right now. And we want to thank Venezuela for that. And we're working very well with them [Acting President Delcy Rodriguez and her government], obviously, or they wouldn't have been so generous.”

At that January 9, meeting, Trump also announced his Executive Order, Safeguarding Venezuelan Oil Revenue for the Good of the American and Venezuelan People under which Venezuelan oil revenues were to be held in a Venezuela Custody Account (VCA) set up by the U.S. Treasury. The VCA was initially based in a Qatar bank, but moved to Citibank in New York in late January. Distribution of the funds for use by the Venezuelan government would be determined by the Secretary of State.

Last week’s KPMG report showed that VCA in January received $500 million. On January 28, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee the payment of $300 million had already been made from the VCA “to keep [Venezuelan] sanitation workers, police officers, government workers on staff,” and that it was from Venezuelan oil sales totaling $500 million.

The KPMG report also showed the VCA received $1 billion in February, another $1.5 billion, and another $2.1 billion in April.

On April 16, the State Department’s Michael Kozak, a senior official from the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs, in testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, disclosed “around $3 billion” of Venezuelan oil revenue had moved through the VCA “paying the salaries of government workers in Venezuela; buying supplies for their oil industry, and so on, other things that benefit the public.”

Since it appears that the VCA did not receive as much as $4 billion until April, that again raises the question what happened to the $4 billion in Venezuelan oil Trump said was “on the way” to the U.S. in early January.

Overall, The KPMG report showed that between January and September 30, 2026, the VCA received $12.26 billion from sales primarily of Venezuelan crude oil and petroleum transactions, with minor amounts from gold, minerals, and fertilizer. In turn, following review and approval by the State Department and Treasury, some $12.11 billion has gone to the Venezuelan central bank or directly to vendors.

As mentioned above, another flow of Venezuelan oil money to the U.S. is coming from the most unusual “historic oil agreement” Trump announced built around the interim Venezuelan government granting what a White House August 31 fact sheet said was “100-year concessions for 17 oil fields with proven reserves of approximately 65 billion barrels” to a company named North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP).

I should point out any 100 year oil concession violates Venezuelan law.

According to a September 2, White House fact sheet, the 17 oil fields were “previously controlled or operated by Russian and Chinese firms, or by corrupt cronies of Maduro and Chavez.”

More important was that the Trump administration signed a joint agreement with NABEP’s parent company, based in Barbados, that grants the U.S. government a 35%-stake in ownership in that corporate parent and the right to buy 20% of NABEP’s Venezuelan oil output at production cost.

Here is the way the September 2, White House fact sheet described that deal. It said the joint agreement “was signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth,” and “at no cost to the American taxpayer, NABEP has granted the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35% equity stake in its corporate parent, representing up to hundreds of billions in value and dividends for the United States.”

In addition, the White House release said, “NABEP has granted the U.S. Department of State the right to purchase, at production cost, a guaranteed 20% of the off-take from all current and future fields NABEP will operate.”

That means that a Pentagon agency is the over one-third owner of a major Venezuelan oil company and the State Department may be the substantial buyer of the oil output of that company. In short, two departments of the U.S. government are now in the oil business.

The September White House release made the further points that, “This is a deal with a private company – not the Venezuelan interim government. It’s not a deal with the interim

In an October 20, report, ProPublica, which said its staff had “reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth,” points out, “The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent [Barbados] company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.”

In short, the public ought to know who are the new business partners of the U.S. Government?

ProPublica also questioned NABEP’s chief executive, Alejandro Betancourt, whom it describes as “a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.”

The agreement gives the U.S. government veto power over the appointment of any member of NABEP’s seven-member board of directors and a majority must be U.S. citizens. ProPublica says the board members have 15-year terms, a move it was told “designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.” Betancourt is the only board member named by the agreement.

According to ProPublica, “The signed agreement is marked as a ‘sensitive’ government document. That classification is commonly used to shield a variety of federal records from public release, including those containing personnel information, details about ongoing law enforcement operations and matters protected by attorney-client privilege. The document also contains a confidentiality clause barring Betancourt’s company from disclosing the ‘existence and terms” of the U.S. government agreement.”

Hopefully, the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress will include the Venezuelan oil deal in one of its investigations.

Meanwhile, on October 27, Trump diverted from a campaign appearance in Texas to make a statement that day pier-side in Corpus Christi, along with Rubio, where two tankers carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan crude produced by NABEP had arrived.

Betancourt was on hand to say, “This first shipment since the U.S.-NABEP deal will be followed by thousands of such arrivals, and each one shows the world that Venezuela is back as a dependable energy supplier, with the United States as its anchor buyer.”

Trump told the press, “We took over Venezuela very successfully and they've sent me as a gift a boatload of a million barrels of oil and I'm giving that to the United States.”

Three days later, Reuters reported, “NABEP initially said the oil was delivered under Washington's right to buy a portion of the company's production at cost. It later said it gave the shipment to the U.S. at no cost to U.S. taxpayer ‘to recognize the historic nature of the agreement.’"

This is an oil agreement worth following.

item.title: The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve
item.description:
The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve Expert comment jon.wallace 17 November 2026

This week’s summit did not produce the Code many desire. But as ASEAN Chair Manila has laid a useful foundation for the Code, while making important progress on regional connectivity.

When it assumed the Chair of ASEAN last year, the Philippines placed negotiations to establish a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) at the centre of its agenda. An agreement has been desired for decades, to help reduce territorial and other tensions between China and regional countries. The need for the COC is clear: Philippine ships have continued to clash with Chinese Coast Guard vessels throughout the year, around disputed areas such as Scarborough Shoal. 

But Philippines Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro cooled expectations of an agreement at this week’s ASEAN summit. In a recent statement, she said that while around 80 per cent of the provisions are agreed, ‘sticking points’ still remain. It is therefore unlikely to be concluded by the end of the year with Philippines as ASEAN Chair.

But the Philippines tenure has been about more than just the COC. In a region of diverging priorities, security alignments, and threat perceptions, Manila should be judged by how far it has boosted ASEAN’s utility as an independent diplomatic actor able to strengthen regional solidarity.

Progress under pressure

The role of ASEAN Chair was clearly going to test the Philippines: How would it reconcile its national security interests with its responsibilities as the leader of a forum for regional cooperation? And would Beijing see Manila as a good faith actor on the COC?

The Philippines is, after all, one of the oldest treaty partners of the US. Those ties are getting stronger under President Ferdinand ‘Bongbong’ Marcos, while its relationship with China becomes ever more fractious – a stance not shared by all ASEAN partners. 

Beside these obvious impediments, the overlapping and complex nature of the claims in South China Sea waters made the COC a tricky subject to negotiate within the bloc, let alone with China. But under the stewardship of the Philippines delegations met every month this year and have managed to produce a substantial part of an agreement – a significant jump after two decades of diplomatic deadlock. 

There is no official confirmation on what the sticking points were, but past statements suggest issues around legal implementation, geographical scope, and terms of reference prevented a final agreement. Singapore, next year’s chair, enjoys a more stable relationship with Beijing and may stand a better chance of ironing out these final elements. Even this remains uncertain, but setting up Singapore with the best possible chance always looked like the most realistic ambition for the Philippines on the COC, and it has made good progress to that end. 

Outside of COC negotiations, the Philippines has managed to make significant moves on some other stated priorities. The Philippines assumed the Chair of ASEAN under the theme ‘Navigating our future, together’. This focussed on three core pillars: Peace and security anchors, prosperity corridors, and people empowerment. 

To this end, Manila concluded negotiations of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA). This is the world’s first binding region-wide digital economy deal, which will better integrate the region and foster greater cross-border data flows and end-to-end digital trade, promising to bring in $2 trillion by 2030. 

The Philippines also championed the ASEAN Leaders’ Declaration on Strategic Trade Management, which aims to establish unified frameworks to strengthen the resilience of regional supply chains. 

And it established the ASEAN Centre of Excellence for Creative Industries, fostering a more interconnected creative economy and greater cultural exchange. Manila has also pushed for greater collaboration on disaster preparedness, with a focus on pooling resources in the face of natural calamities.

One significant area where little has been achieved is the crisis in Myanmar: diplomatic progress on the issue was a strategic and symbolic challenge for the Philippines and ASEAN’s credibility as a peace-making body. In the end, ASEAN’s agenda remains stalled. The summit agreed to pursue ‘calibrated engagement’ in pursuit of ASEAN’s ‘5 Point Consensus’, and leaves the door open for gradual restoration to the bloc. But as a unified group, ASEAN appears to have little hope of influencing Myanmar’s military government.

Successful summitry 

This summit needed to go well for President Marcos. The Philippines has been pursuing its ASEAN agenda at a time of mounting domestic pressure. The war in Iran has strained energy supply chains, hindering access to necessities. Summer saw massive losses from tsunamis and earthquakes, and impeachment proceedings against the Vice President. The Marcos administration received its lowest ever approval ratings this month, as protestors clashed with police on the eve of the summit. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

The event was ostensibly been productive. More than 150 outcome documents were reviewed and approved. A new ASEAN free trade agreement has been agreed with Canada. Brazil and Canada have committed $540 million for rainforest protection. And the event presented a significant opportunity for the bloc to interact with influential leaders including President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Prime Minister Mark Carney, and President Lula da Silva.

And as always at summits, meetings on the sidelines provided opportunities for important diplomacy: Japan’s PM Takaichi and South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung held their fourth bilateral meeting. And the Quad convened for the first time in two years. 

But ASEAN countries must see real returns from these convenings to be considered a success. And it is imperative that ASEAN as a unit is seen as a key player rather than a platform through which bilateral deals can be done. Indeed, Philippines President Marcos emphasized a ‘whole-of-ASEAN approach’ in his plenary speech.

This focus on unifying regional interests is not for the sake of ASEAN alone, but part of a wider strategy to protect the Philippines in the face of broader geopolitical trends. The test will be if Manila can carry this sentiment forward beyond its tenure as chair – something that may prove difficult.

Preparing for the storms ahead

2027 will see Singapore become ASEAN Chair with the organization set to be tested by deepening faultlines on AI alliances, critical mineral exploration, and supply chain and energy resilience. 

Divergences are already appearing among members on how best to approach these issues. Coming on top of existing territorial disputes, strained relations within the bloc seem likely. However, even if ASEAN countries have diverging interests, they will never be able to escape the reality of what they share: geography and history. 

As the overlapping threats of climate change, great power rivalry, and an unstable global economy demand a cohesive regional response, the Philippines’ priorities of cohesion and greater interdependence will be key to the region’s survival. What this year has made clear is that grand international dealmaking of the kind represented by the COC may continue to prove difficult for the group. Despite this, ASEAN can provide an indispensable function, facilitating interoperability and integration that fuels growth and secures sovereignty. 

As President Marcos said at the summit’s opening, the coming years will be about ‘not only where ASEAN is headed, but what ASEAN must become’. For years the ASEAN has been dismissed as ineffectual and underperforming. But the group has endured. And the Philippines period as Chair has perhaps shown the bloc’s true value – driving incremental but unyielding change towards an increasingly interconnected region.
